A loan against property (LAP) is secured borrowing against real estate you own — residential, commercial or land. A loan against property where the security is residential — a self-occupied or let-out house or flat. Residential property is generally the most straightforward security to value, so lenders often apply their most favourable LTV within LAP.

A loan secured against a motorcycle or scooter. Ticket sizes are small and tenures short, so approval is often quicker than for larger vehicle finance, though the same hypothecation and insurance rules apply.

A loan secured against a plot of land rather than a built property. Because vacant land produces no income and can be harder to sell, lenders apply the most conservative LTV in the LAP family and are selective about location and title.

A loan secured against commercial real estate — a shop, office, warehouse or other business premises. Lenders usually apply a more conservative LTV than for residential property, because commercial assets can be slower to sell.

A loan secured by pledging financial assets — shares, mutual funds, bonds or deposits. You keep ownership and continue to receive dividends or growth, while the lender holds a lien. It is typically structured as an overdraft, so interest applies only to what you draw.

A loan to buy a pre-owned car. The lender values the vehicle, and its age and condition drive both the amount advanced and the tenure allowed. Rates sit above new-car finance because used vehicles are harder to value and resell.

A loan to buy plant, machinery or equipment, secured against the asset itself. Because the lender holds security, terms are usually better than unsecured business borrowing, and the tenure is matched to the useful life of the asset.
